content.user_title: Apply CQS and CQRS Patterns in .NET
content.value_statement: Teams often mix state changes and data reads, which makes code harder to test and reason about. This skill guides clear CQS and CQRS designs for .NET methods, handlers, and controllers.
actual_capabilities: Explains the difference between commands that change state and queries that return data.
Provides C# examples for method-level CQS violations and corrected designs.
Shows CQRS command, query, handler, dispatcher, and controller patterns.
Lists practical exceptions such as atomic operations, fluent APIs, and factory methods.
Helps decide when CQRS is useful and when simple CRUD is enough.
limitations: Focuses on .NET and C# examples, not other language ecosystems.
Does not provide a complete production framework or package.
Does not cover database migration, deployment, or infrastructure setup.
Requires users to adapt examples to their domain model and persistence layer.

use_cases.title: Separate Service Methods
use_cases.description: Review service methods that both modify state and return domain data, then split them into clearer commands and queries.

use_cases.title: Design CQRS Handlers
use_cases.description: Create command and query records with matching handlers for a .NET application layer.

use_cases.title: Review Architecture Complexity
use_cases.description: Decide whether a feature needs CQRS or whether simpler CRUD patterns are more appropriate.

prompt_templates.title: Identify CQS Violations
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review of a method or class.
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this .NET class for CQS violations. Identify methods that both change state and return data, then suggest simpler names and responsibilities.

prompt_templates.title: Refactor to Commands and Queries
prompt_templates.prompt: Refactor this service API into separate command and query operations. Keep behavior equivalent and explain each new responsibility.

prompt_templates.title: Design a CQRS Application Layer
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a CQRS application layer for this feature. Include command records, query records, handler responsibilities, and controller flow.

prompt_templates.title: Evaluate CQRS Tradeoffs
prompt_templates.prompt: Assess whether CQRS fits this system. Compare benefits, added complexity, testing impact, read model needs, and alternatives.

output_examples.input: A stack class has one method that removes and returns the top item.
output: The method mixes a command and a query.
Use one operation to inspect the top item and a separate operation to remove it.
This keeps repeated reads safe and makes state changes explicit.

output_examples.input: An order feature needs create, cancel, lookup, and customer order list operations.
output: Create and cancel are commands because they change state.
Lookup and list operations are queries because they return data without side effects.
Separate handlers make validation, persistence, and read optimization easier to test.

output_examples.input: A small CRUD admin page is being considered for CQRS.
output: CQRS may add unnecessary complexity for a simple admin workflow.
Use it only if read and write models have meaningfully different needs.
A standard service or controller may be enough.

best_practices: Name commands with imperative verbs and queries with read-oriented names.
Keep queries free of side effects so they are safe to repeat.
Use CQRS when read and write paths have different models, scale, or rules.
anti_patterns: Returning full domain objects from methods that also persist changes.
Adding CQRS to simple CRUD screens without a clear need.
Hiding state changes inside getters, calculated properties, or query handlers.

faq.question: What problem does this skill solve?
faq.answer: It helps teams separate state-changing operations from read operations in .NET code.

faq.question: Does it generate production-ready code?
faq.answer: It provides design guidance and examples that users must adapt to their application.

faq.question: Is CQS the same as CQRS?
faq.answer: No. CQS is a method-level principle, while CQRS separates read and write models at the architecture level.

faq.question: When should I avoid CQRS?
faq.answer: Avoid CQRS for simple CRUD workflows where separate read and write models do not add value.

faq.question: Can commands return identifiers?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill treats returning an identifier from a command as an acceptable practical exception.
